title: Notes of Ministry - 71 - October 1978

paragraphs.text: Peter writes to sojourners dispersed in certain Roman provinces far from their homeland. He refers to them in chapter 2 as “strangers and sojourners” (1 Peter 2: 11). I suppose they would have no rights in the countries in which they were living; they were strangers below and citizens above. They would have no influence on the course of this world; they were in the world but not of it. They were not of the world but in it to testify, and for the pleasure and the will of God. That is our position as believers—we are in the world but we are not meant to belong to it, we are meant to be apart from it. Our citizenship is in heaven, and yet we are left here in the world for the pleasure of God and for testimony.

Although they are addressed as sojourners and strangers they are addressed also as “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1 Peter 1: 2). Although they would not be much thought of in the provinces in which they were, nor be persons of influence or be honoured by their fellow men, they were elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. God the Father had these very persons in purpose before the world’s foundation, which is true of believers down here now. This dignity, dear brethren, belongs to persons who are believers in our Lord Jesus Christ. The Lord Jesus Himself is the Elect; “Mine elect”. God said as to Him
(Isaiah 42: 1); it is special to Him; He is unique as God’s Elect; yet these persons were elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father.

Peter adds, “by sanctification of the Spirit”. Not only were they in God’s mind before the world’s foundation but they were persons who had received the Holy Spirit in view of being sanctified, set apart for holy purposes. That is our place down here, “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, by sanctification of the Spirit”. The elect come to light as set apart by sanctification of the Spirit. I understand that the word “elect” applies to the words that follow—“according to” and “by” and “unto”; “unto the obedience, and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”. The end in view is that persons are to be obedient. Indeed the same persons are addressed in 1 Peter 1: 14 as “children of obedience”; they belong to that family.

“Unto the obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”, that is, the blood of Jesus Christ has certain claims upon these persons and they are desirous of answering to the claims that the blood has upon them.

In Leviticus 8 the blood of the ram of consecration was put on the tip of the right ear, on the thumb of the right hand, and on the great toe of the right foot of the priests, and the oil was put on these same members. I think we need to represent a fulness of committal and devotion in the day in which we live. There was never a time for half measures, nor for having one foot self-pleasing and one foot in the will of God. It is impossible really; it is an unsatisfactory state to be in. What the Lord is after is fulness of committal to Him and to the will of God. The cleansed leper also had the blood put upon the tip of the right ear, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the

great toe of his right foot (Leviticus 14: 14). We are all, I trust, cleansed lepers; we have known what it is to do our own will, even as believers, but there is a way of repentance and cleansing. The same treatment as in the consecration of the priests was given in the cleansing of the leper. It is in view of being set apart “by sanctification of the Spirit, unto the obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”.

In 1 Peter 3: 18 Peter says, “Christ indeed has once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God”. It is a great matter to be brought to God, to be brought from our own matters, our own things, our own interests, and brought to God, brought in view of being serviceable to God and committed to His will. I had especially in mind the opening verses of chapter 4. It says there, “Christ, then, having suffered for us in the flesh, do ye also arm yourselves with the same mind; for he that has suffered in the flesh has done with sin”.

The question, dear brethren, is whether we are prepared to suffer rather than sin. It is a test for every one of us. What will help us is our positive link with a living Man in heaven who, as it says at the end of chapter 3, “is at the right hand of God, gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being subjected to him”. The Lord Jesus Christ holds the highest office in the universe; no one surpasses Him as to the office which He fills, angels and authorities and powers being subjected to Him. How blessed to have Him before us as the object of our faith and our affections, and to be held, to abide in Him in that sense.
Then as we consider the fact that He suffered for sins we are by the Spirit’s help brought round to preferring to suffer rather than sin, to prefer to do God’s will rather than do our own.
What a

practical matter it is, to prefer to please God rather than to please ourselves, to prefer to be deprived of certain things that would please us. Not only is it wrong to sin, but the Spirit would help us to prefer to suffer rather than sin. Our tastes are to come round to this view that we would prefer to suffer rather than sin; we prefer God’s will to our will; we prefer to be pleasing to God rather than please ourselves; we prefer to be deprived, to deprive ourselves of certain things that please us, in order to be here for the pleasure of God. This is how the elect, dear brethren, come to light. A few of the elect in New York are here; such persons are dignified. They are certainly not all here tonight; there are many elect in New York; but the great challenge is whether we are showing that we are elect, whether there is with us this
“sanctification of the Spirit, unto the obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”.

It comes out in these features I have mentioned that we prefer certain things, prefer God’s will to our own will. None of us is like that naturally, not one of us; it goes against nature; but may the Lord help every one of us to desire to have this kind of taste, this kind of desire, to please God rather than please ourselves. May the Lord help us.

I wondered if we could just take account of these three men who resorted to the presence of God. They would be examples for us. It is wonderful that the presence of God is available to us, that is, He desires men to resort to Him, not only in need but at any time. We sang yesterday about the matchless grace that finds delight in men. The whole purpose and working out of God’s ways is in view of His tabernacling with men, a wonderful thing.
‘That Thou should’st take delight in me,
Yet be the God Thou art,
Is darkness to my intellect
But sunshine to my heart’.

Daniel resorted to the presence of God in a time of crisis. We know that it was his habit to resort there, but the verse reads, “And when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and, his windows being open in his upper chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime”. The detail is remarkable. He was not overwhelmed by the crisis. It is always a test to us as to how we behave in a crisis; it brings out where we are; it brings out the work of God, or it brings out the absence of the work of God. The attack was on Daniel here but he realised that the attack was against God. It is an amazing thing that these men had planned to annihilate the thought of men approaching God. You think of the audacity of the enemy, for he has not small ideas. Paul says, “We are not ignorant of his thoughts”, 2 Corinthians 2: 11.

They had actually planned to annihilate the matter of men resorting to the presence of God. In the crisis Daniel resorts there just as he had always done. Even in the midst of Babylon he had an upper chamber and his windows were open towards Jerusalem. In his prayer in chapter 9 he speaks of God’s sanctuary; that was in his heart, not his own safety. God can change the course of nature if it is a matter of the safety of His people, but in this section it is the way in which God comes in for the protecting of this matter of approach to Himself.

In 2 Samuel 7 David went in and sat before Jehovah. It says of Daniel that he kneeled. Daniel had not an official place to go to, he went to his house, and it was a little sanctuary in Babylon where he could approach God. But David went in and sat restfully before Jehovah and that at the time of the greatest disappointment that he could have experienced. From his earliest days he had in mind “a place for Jehovah, habitations for the Mighty One of Jacob”, Psalm 132: 5. It filled his thoughts; his objective was God’s rest and God’s service. But he gets the word through Nathan that he was not to build the house, and we see how he carries himself in the disappointment. Things had not gone just quite the way he wanted them to go.

He wanted to see things filled out and prospering in his locality, as it were, in his area of things, but it did not quite go that way. He got light, of course, as to Christ typically, light as to sonship, light as to Solomon, that he was to build the house. You delight in the way he takes it, the way he bows to God’s sovereign choice of the son to build the house of Jehovah.

The brethren know this passage well, how he expresses his own thoughts of God, the names and titles he uses and the wealth that enters into it. It seems to be the result of the way that he took the word of God. So he went in and sat before Jehovah. He is perfectly restful as to the matter of God going to work out His own thoughts in His own way.
Then in Numbers 7 it is a time of wonderful prosperity. It was on the very day that Moses had completed the setting up of the tabernacle that these princes came forward with their offerings of

such wealth. It must have been a marvellous moment in the history of Moses. The work was complete in accordance with the commandment of Jehovah, every detail in accord with the pattern, and it had been brought to Moses to come under his scrutiny. It was a time of wonderful prosperity. In some sense there was never a day in Israel like it, it is like Pentecostal times, when everything was secured in its first flush of glory, the glory coming in and filling the tabernacle, and these princes coming forward with all their wealth, dedicating it to the service of God. It was at that point that Moses went in to speak with Him. It does not say that he went in to pray, he just went in to speak with God. There was wonderful nearness and intimacy as he went in there in relation to the fulfilment of the divine thoughts in the people of God. The heart of Moses must have been filled and satisfied.

But as he goes in he heard the voice speaking to him from off the mercy-seat. What he discovers is that the great purpose of this whole arrangement, the tabernacle system, was that God should have a place where He could speak, where His voice would be heard, as He had said in Exodus 25: 22, “There will I meet with thee, and will speak with thee”. A wonderful moment had arrived for God when He had conditions and a place and a throne in the midst of His people. God spoke to Moses, and then Moses spoke to Him. Moses, as it were, takes the second place. He had gone in to speak with Him, but God claims the right to speak in His house. Then what comes out is that, whatever results have been secured in the people, everything must relate to Christ—“When thou lightest the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light over against the candlestick”. God says, as it were, If this result is to be maintained, everything has to centre in Christ, every
light has to be related to Christ. I trust we may be encouraged in these things.

This scripture in John 13 was referred to in the reading on Lord’s day and in reflecting on it I have been impressed with the greatness of the service of feet-washing and its importance in the mind of the Lord Jesus. It comes in in the final phase of His days here and at the threshold of these chapters in which He unfolds so much to His own as to the great thoughts of God. He could have instructed the disciples to do it, but the fact that He does it by way of example shows how important it is in His mind. Our brother prayed for good conditions in local assemblies, and the practice of this service of feet-washing is essential to good conditions amongst the saints. In performing this service what is in the mind of the Lord Jesus is that we might be freed from defilement that we gather in the wilderness during the course of fulfilling our righteous obligations, also that we may be refreshed in view of proceeding restfully and in liberty into what He speaks of as “part with me”, that is, part with Him in relation to all that is for the pleasure of God, and part with Him too in the sphere of testimony.
I do feel impressed with the importance of this service in the Lord’s mind. Indeed, I think it is safe to say that the Lord Jesus is the only Person recorded in Scripture who actually took water and

washed the feet of others. Men like Abraham, Lot, Laban, and the man over Joseph’s house all provided water for others to wash their own feet, and Abigail showed a delightful spirit, the spirit of Christ, when she said, “Let thy handmaid be a bondwoman to wash the feet of the servants of my lord” (1 Samuel 25: 41), but the Spirit does not record her actually doing it.
Then the woman in Luke 7 washed the feet of Jesus with tears.

As far as I can recall the Lord Himself is the only One whom the Spirit records as actually taking water and performing this service, and He gives it in great detail, which shows its greatness and importance. John would be affected by the greatness of Christ’s Person as he wrote these words—“Jesus, knowing that the Father had given him all things into his hands, and that he came out from God and was going to God”, also when he wrote the opening words of this gospel—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”. You can understand that his soul would be deeply moved as he thought,

‘That Person washed my feet’. The human mind would regard this as a very menial service, but, beloved brethren, it is a service that has been ennobled by the greatness of the Person who has set it on by way of example. This service is also great by reason of the greatness of the persons whose feet are being washed, the saints, the brethren of Christ, the sons of God.

How attractive this should make it to us! Jesus “lays aside his garments”. There is nothing official about it. Indeed, it is the service of a bondman, and the Lord Jesus has glorified the matter of bondmanship in “taking a bondman’s form”, Philippians.2: 7. The Hebrew bondman, that wonderful type of Christ, said distinctly, “I love my master, my wife, and my children”. Ah, dear brethren, it is the way that love would serve others, as Paul says, “By love serve one another”
(Galatians 5: 13), and the Lord is setting the matter on by way of example and not as a picture on the wall.

It is service by personal contact. John does not care for “paper and ink”, he prefers “mouth to mouth”, 2 John 12. It is a service in love in which we are to be impartial, for Jesus was impartial. He washed the feet of all the disciples. As He proceeds with this service, Peter objects, but it is not in mind to speak on that but of what the Lord Jesus says—“Unless I wash thee, thou hast not part with me”. In these chapters, John 13–17, the Lord unfolds great things, as also in His message in John 20: 17—“I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. So He says, “If I therefore, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet; for I have given you an example that, as I have done to you, ye should do also”. He has given the example, and His mind is that we should continue this service to one another as normal practice in the same way and same spirit during His absence. This makes for good assembly relations and conditions so that, in restfulness and liberty, we can enter upon and enjoy together our part with Christ in relation to the greatest and most precious things of God.

The scripture read in 1 Timothy 5: 5 relates to an individual, a widow indeed, but I wish to apply it to our present position publicly. The severe exercises we have been through and the sorrowful loss of numbers have brought home to us that our position publicly is what is described here as “a widow indeed”; not simply “a widow”, but “a widow indeed”. We are surrounded by a vast profession which bears the name of Christ but which is heartless as to Him and says in her heart, “I sit a queen, and I am not a widow”, Revelation 18: 7. As we think of this,

and the Lord’s holy feelings in regard of it, let us be exercised to be wholly free of every element of pretension, for it becomes us to bear the features of the “widow indeed” as set out in this verse—“left alone”; we have no outward resources or means of support, for Christ, our Husband, is absent. She “has put her hope in God”; we have no earth-bound prospect, our outlook is for the coming of Christ, and we await the glory of God. She “continues in supplications and prayers night and day”; we are to be marked by constant, sustained dependence on God in a world of independence of God, and in the midst of a lukewarm profession which assumes to have need of nothing (Revelation 3: 17).

Yet in the inside circle precious features are to operate in love, as we read in verse 10. The inside circle of John 13 to 17 is a wonderful thing, the circle of the saints where love is active and operative. In this circle the children are brought up, not left to grow up, but brought up.

They are protected, cherished, and nourished, as it says in the previous chapter, “nourished with the words of the faith and of the good teaching” (verse 6). What an environment for the young to be brought up in, where all that is of the world that crucified Christ is absolutely excluded and only what is of Christ promoted! Hospitality is to be exercised. It is a great privilege to entertain the saints, “the excellent”, of whom Christ says, “In them is all my delight” (Psalm 16: 3), and to use our means on the principle of stewardship in the practical support of the testimony.

Then the saints’ feet are to be washed. The very fact that numbers have been so reduced should cause us to value each other all the more and give us to see the importance of serving one another in love in the same spirit in which our Lord and

Teacher has set the example, with a view to our enjoying together our part with Christ. The presence of our brethren with us here these past few days has refreshed us, our feet have been washed, and on Lord’s day morning we enjoyed together our part with Christ in that realm where all subsists for the pleasure and glory of God, ‘in that world surpassing great’, as was expressed in the last hymn we sang. May we be encouraged to continue, as our normal practice, this service of love to one another, so that our part with Christ may be enjoyed together in a fuller way in these days of “widow indeed” character publicly.

This occasion of which we have read would be similar to the occasion we are having this afternoon—a meeting in a house. The word rapidly travelled round that the Lord Jesus was at this house or, as the note says, ‘at home’. The Spirit tells us that the house was packed, “no longer any room, not even at the door”. And there was a needy person outside who wanted the help that Jesus alone could give to him, and he could not get near to Him.
The old hymn says, ‘I wish I had been with Him then’, when He took the little children in His arms and laid His hands upon them. I think we can understand the sentiments expressed in that hymn,

that it would have been a unique experience to be with Jesus when He was here on earth; but you would have been subject to the difficulties that this poor man had. You might have found it very difficult to get near to Him. Now that He is in the glory He cannot be seen with our natural eyes as we could have seen Him if we had lived when He was here, but it is possible to get near to Jesus. There is no need to go to the lengths that these men had to go to. It is possible to get near to Jesus this afternoon, and the gospel is preached to that end, that you might come to know Him, come to receive a touch from Him if you have never received one before. And even if you have received one before, it is intended that you should receive a fresh touch from Him.

It is possible to get near to Him because He Himself has drawn near to us. In coming into manhood, in coming down from His seat on high, from that exalted position, He has come into the circumstances in which we are, that He might draw near to us. It is wonderful grace that He being who He is should be prepared to draw near to us. Persons who lived with Him were amazed at the company that He kept; they were amazed that sinners and tax gatherers came to Him and that He ate with them. He was criticized because He was seen in the company of needy persons and, beloved, He is still presented in the gospel as available and willing to help needy persons. If we had read the end of the previous chapter we would have read about a leper who said, “If thou wilt thou canst cleanse me”. We need to be assured that Jesus is willing to help. There was no doubt with these persons that brought the paralytic that He was not only willing but that He had the resource to help, and that if this man was to get blessing, if he was to be healed, it could only be by a touch from Jesus.

It is still the same this afternoon. If you are to receive the blessing of the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit these things can only be had by a personal transaction with Jesus. You might come, to the gospel preaching, and it is good that you do, you might feel refreshment of spirit sitting and listening to the word, but blessing for your soul can only be received by having to do with Jesus for yourself. The preacher of the gospel cannot give you faith, still less can he forgive your sins. Your mother and father may themselves have received the blessing of the gospel, and they may long and pray that you should receive it, but they could never forgive your sins, nor could they pass on to you the faith that they themselves have received. These things are only received by a personal transaction with Jesus. It is a very wonderful thing to be under the sound of the word as this great company of persons was. It says that He spoke the word to them. The word of God in the gospel is a signpost. It directs you to the place where blessing can be received, and blessing can be received alone in Jesus.

If you think of salvation, there is no other “name under heaven which is given among men by which we must be saved”, Acts 4: 12. If we think of redemption, it is “the redemption which is in Christ Jesus”, Romans 3: 24. If you go through the Scriptures and think of all the blessings that God so richly gives, you will discover that they are all connected with the Person of Jesus. Nothing for God has been secured outside of that blessed Man, and no blessing for man can be received without Him, no blessing at all. If you are without God, if you are without Christ, then you are without God and without hope. What a terrible predicament to be in in a dispensation of grace when God is so richly and so freely blessing men in Christ. So the gospel is preached that you
might come to Him. The word ‘come’ is a gospel word, it is an evangelical word, a word uttered by the Lord Jesus Himself; He said, “Come to me, all ye who labour and are burdened”, Matthew 11: 28.

The woman in John 4 had to do with Him for herself and then she went away and bore testimony as to what she had found; she gave evidence that she had met One who had told her all things that she had ever done and she says to the men of the city, “Is not he the Christ?”.

Because of her word “They went out of the city and came to him”. But they very quickly came back and said to the woman, “It is no longer on account of thy saying that we believe, for we have heard him ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world”.
So the testimony goes out that He is the Christ; God has made Him both Lord and Christ.
God has installed Him in a place of power and dominion, and the invitation in the gospel is that we each should have to do with Him for ourselves.

It is very wonderful that these persons were concerned to bring this man to Jesus. He would never have got there if he had been left to his own devices. He was a paralytic, unable to move, unable to help himself, and that is our condition if we are still in our sins, unable to help ourselves, no sign of life towards God, paralytic. And yet there were persons there who were concerned for his soul. It is a wonderful thing if there are persons concerned for our souls, concerned that we might be brought to Jesus—persons who themselves cannot impart the blessing to us but are concerned that we should have it for ourselves. Mother and father may be those who would bring us to Jesus from an early age. They would teach us about Jesus, what He has done and where He is. And brethren who love us and know us would be those who would bring us to
Jesus, who would desire that we should have this inward secret transaction with Himself.

This man had friends, four of them, who were prepared to go to great lengths to bring him to Jesus, and it says of Jesus that He saw their faith. Later on, as to the scribes, it says that He knew their reasonings. You see, He hears and He sees; He takes account of things that may not be apparent to others, and the reason is that He looks into our hearts.

This afternoon as we sit listening to the gospel preaching He looks into our hearts and He sees what effect the word is having there, whether there is a spirit of disbelief that refuses the word, or whether there is a listening in faith. It says of some persons that the word preached to them did not profit them, “not being mixed with faith in those who heard”, Hebrews 4: 2.
He looked at these four persons and saw their faith. It would be a wonderful thing if He could look into our hearts this afternoon, each one of us in this room, and see active faith there.

Faith is God’s gift. Of course, it is man’s responsibility to believe the gospel, but then man’s responsibility and God’s sovereignty go along together. If God enjoins all men everywhere to repent, as He does, He also grants repentance, it is His gift. He grants softening of heart towards Himself and repentance. If the gospel is preached for the obedience of faith, as it is, that too is God’s gift. Scripture tells us that we are “saved by grace, through faith; and this not of yourselves; it is God’s gift”, Ephesians 2: 8.

So God expects me to believe what He tells me in the gospel because it is God who says it, but He gives me faith to receive the word. What wondrous grace that is! If we find it difficult to believe the gospel, if we find it difficult to put confidence

and trust in Jesus, we can ask God for faith. God is waiting to be asked for the greatest gifts; they are given to people who ask for them. Children are often taught at home that they are not to ask for things, but divine things are there for persons who ask for them, who ask for faith, who ask for the Holy Spirit, another of God’s gifts, described in the Scriptures as God’s unspeakable free gift (2 Corinthians 9: 15).

So these men had faith—and the Lord Jesus forgave the paralytic’s sins. I suppose what this man was primarily hoping for was relief from his paralysis, but the Lord Jesus forgave his sins. If we are going to have to do with Jesus for ourselves, then He would have to do with us first about our sins. I wonder if every one of us in this room has had to do with Him about our sins? Let us not be in any doubt that there are some upon our conscience, but then we can have to do with Jesus and have them all righteously forgiven. We can have a conscience that is freed of guilt, so that we are no longer bowed down by a sense of inadequacy, or by the fear of death and of judgment to come. A conscience freed of guilt is what the believer is to have and the gospel is preached to that end, that the blessing that this man received should be received by each of us. “Thy sins”, He says, “are forgiven thee”. There were persons there who were critical; they did not believe that the One who forgave sins had the right to forgive them and they said—and what they said is quite right—that the only Person who can forgive sins is God Himself. I wonder if we believe that.
You might do something against me, and I might be prepared to forgive you, but the forgiveness of the sin rests with God alone. Every sin is an affront to Him, an affront to His majesty. It is
the operation of a will that is contrary to His, therefore it is lawlessness (1 John 3: 4).

Therefore it is with God that we have to do about our sins, and every man, woman, and child that has ever lived will have to do with God some time about their sins. God in the gospel is inviting us to have to do with Him about them this afternoon. He says, “Now is the well-accepted time; behold, now the day of salvation”, Hebrews 6: 2. Through the prophet Isaiah He says, “Come now, let us reason together, saith Jehovah—though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be white as snow”, Isaiah 1: 18. God is giving an invitation to guilty sinners in the gospel to have to do with Him about their sins because He has a righteous basis on which to justify them. The man who went up into the temple to pray was so overcome by the burden of his guilt and need that he did not even lift up his eyes to heaven, such was his guilt, but he smote upon his breast and said, “O God, have compassion on me, the sinner”, Luke 18: 13.

Oh how wonderful it is to experience divine mercy! That is all the sinner can ask, you know; he cannot claim forgiveness of sins as a right, he rests entirely upon the sovereignty of divine mercy, mercy which is freely bestowed because God is rich in it. God is rich in mercy, and He delights in justifying the repenting sinner. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and cleanse us from all unrighteousness”, 1 John 1: 9. How unqualified that statement is! The guilty sinner can go out of the presence of God without a stain upon him. Justification means that the sinner is set up as if he has never sinned at all.
God is able to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
But persons who will not have to do with God

about their sins in this dispensation of blessing will have to do with Him about them in a time of judgment. I do not go into that, but Scripture is very plain, it says that “each of us shall give an account concerning himself to God” (Romans 14: 12)—each of us. None will be exempt from that, and God will want an account for every sin. Scripture speaks of that terrible scene of judgment, of the dead being summoned before the great white throne. It says that they were judged out of the things written in the books (Revelation 20: 12). That can only spell for them condemnation. The things written in the books will be their life histories, a record of every sin committed, and if God judges sinners by those things it will only be for condemnation. But God is offering to us a righteousness that is by faith of Jesus Christ, so that we can appear in His presence as righteous as Jesus is. A full acceptance before Him can be mine, knowing that God will no longer impute my sins. “Blessed is he”, says David,

“whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered!”, Psalm 32: 1. Blessed indeed is this gift of forgiveness of sins! Let us not underestimate it, let us not regard it as an elementary part of the gospel; it is a great blessing indeed to be freed from one’s sins and to be set up righteously in the divine presence.

Jesus knew that the scribes reasoned thus and He asks a question—“Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, Thy sins are forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and take up thy couch and walk?”. I suppose the persons there looking down at this poor man lying on his couch would have thought that it was a lot easier to say, ‘Thy sins are forgiven thee’, than to say, ‘Get up and walk’ to a man so immobile that he had to be carried by four.
If the man was to be free from his paralysis, if

he was to be cured and set up again, all it required was a word of divine power from the One who brought everything into being. One word of divine power and millions of stars sprang into existence, and that was all—and I say all carefully—that was required if this man was to be freed from his paralysis. But if his sins were to be forgiven much more than that was required. Oh how much was required!

It looked so simple to say it, “Thy sins are forgiven thee”; it looks so blessedly simple this afternoon—God offering the forgiveness of sins. But do you realise, dear friend, how much lies behind it? No word of power could ever forgive this man’s sins. It necessitated that Jesus should come here as a lowly Man; that He should come into the world, as the scripture says, to save sinners; that He should give His life an offering once for all; that He should bear those sins now so freely forgiven, bear them in His body on the tree; that His soul should be made an offering for sin; that He should experience not only the humiliation and hatred and malice of men, but that He should know what it was to be forsaken of God. None of us will ever understand fully what it meant to Jesus to be forsaken of God. His holy soul gave some expression to it prophetically in the psalm, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”, Psalm 22: 1.

I thought of it this morning, that on that night, as the apostle says, when the Lord Jesus was betrayed He instituted the Supper; the night when those that loved Him deserted Him; one who was His familiar friend betraying Him, another whom He loved denying Him with oaths and curses, and the rest of them forsaking Him and fleeing. Think of what that meant to the Saviour, but it was small in comparison with what it meant to Him to be forsaken of God.

He could say to the Father, “I knew that thou always hearest me”, John 11: 42. He rejoiced in spirit as a Man here in His link with the Father, in all that He drew from the Father. What it meant to Him that that link, that communion, so blessed, should be interrupted, we shall never fully understand. God in the gospel is now shining out in benign blessing upon the world, the world that has crucified His beloved Son. But Jesus was forsaken of God and His feelings as to it are given expression to that we might apprehend something of the immense cost that lies behind the great gift of the forgiveness of sins.

He went into death; He died for our sins, and He was buried, and He rose the third day. What testimony there is in the gospel to the One who has been into death and broken its power that He might set free “all those who through fear of death through the whole of their life were subject to bondage”, Hebrews 2: 15. How many persons there are who are in fear of death, who go from day to day in fear of it; for to them it means the end and after it the judgment.

Some choose to speculate about what is after death. The believer knows that these things have been removed from the sphere of speculation. God has stated in the Scripture quite plainly that after death is the judgment (Hebrews 9: 27). Persons who have chosen to ignore the great blessing which is presented at such immense cost will have to account to God for it.

“How shall we escape if we have been negligent of so great salvation?”, Hebrews 2: 3. You might choose, you see, to be negligent of it. You might listen to the gospel even this afternoon and not outrightly disbelieve it or refuse it; but you might choose to put it off to another time. You might think that such things will come your way again. The apostle says,
“How shall we escape if we have been negligent of so great salvation?”.

Well, the blessing is there, the blessing of forgiveness of sins, but, more than that, the gift of the Holy Spirit. This man, having received the blessing of the forgiveness of sins, was made to rise up and take up his couch and walk. No longer was he to be borne about by others, .he was to stand on his own feet in the testimony, he was to take up his own responsibilities in his house. How are we able to do that apart from the gift of the Holy Spirit, God’s unspeakable free gift? All that we receive by faith depends for its present enjoyment on the presence of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us. May God’s word promote exercise of soul and desire with us for these precious things, for His name’s sake.
“We, being many”—who are they
Who, in the Supper, thus are one?
Fruit of His death, who joyful own
Their debt to Him, God’s blessed Son?
“We, being many”—is this true
When scattered they throughout the world,
Of no account, despised and few,
With Satan’s power against them hurled?
Yes, till He comes, the church remains,
Her purpose and her prospect sure;
There rises still to Him above
That cry to greet Him even more.
“The many”—who can those forget
For whom their Lord Himself did die?
Though two or three their souls are set
With Him and all the saints on high.
United then at that last shout
When He, the Lord Himself, shall come,
Caught up “the many” then will be
To share with Him what He has won.
Kingston, Ont.
I understand the glory of God to indicate the completeness of moral perfection in display.

Circumstances have come to pass which have brought the moral perfections of God into display, and they are all proportionate and harmonious. Righteousness, love, holiness, mercy, faithfulness, truth—all that goes to make up the moral perfection of God—all are harmonious. That is the simple idea to my mind of the glory of God, and it is seen in the face of Jesus Christ. It is what Stephen saw, and where Stephen left off Paul begins.
